entry.title: Sitting Target, 1972 - ★★★★
entry.content:
this movie rules. oliver reed is settling in for a long prison stint when his wife visits to tells him she's pregnant with someone else's baby. consumed with the need to kill her for the betrayal, reed escapes from prison with his boyfriend ian mcshane, who spends a lot of the movie having sex with various women while oliver reed looks pained and forlorn nearby. "you'll have to excuse my friend," mcshane says to one woman, "he's feeling a bit queer."

it's an absolute miracle of an oliver reed performance. he's somehow brutal and tender in the exact same moments. he makes ian mcshane look like a twink just by existing. he does a bunch of stunts and works those big beautiful melancholy eyes and buries his face into an empty fur coat like it's the bush of the most intoxicating woman in the world and he's sad about how badly he wants it.

my god!!!

entry.title: The Damned, 1962 - ★★★½
entry.content:
"unhappy dangerous boy"

The Damned opens on the Weymouth esplanade with a gang of teddy boys whistling a pop song whose whole lyric is, basically, "black leather, black leather, smash smash smash." Their leader, King, is not in leather. He wears a tweed jacket and carries a furled umbrella like a guards officer. He is Oliver Reed in his early twenties, using his sister as bait to roll an American tourist.

That's the first reel. Then Joseph Losey walks the film off the promenade and down the cliff into something else entirely: a sculptor's studio on the headland (Viveca Lindfors, working among Elisabeth Frink's real bronzes), a civil servant with a secret, and a classroom of polite children whose skin is cold to the touch.

Reed's King is all appetite and jealousy, too fond of his sister by far, but for once the picture around him is bigger and colder than he is. Nobody has to pretend he is a light comedian (https://letterboxd.com/nonmodernist/film/take-a-girl-like-you-1970/); the film simply has something more frightening in the basement. It is also the least Hammer of Hammer films, moreso even than the next year's Paranoiac: black-and-white 'Scope, shot on the Dorset coast, structured like a trapdoor instead of a corridor (https://letterboxd.com/nonmodernist/film/the-curse-of-the-werewolf/).

entry.title: The Hunting Party, 1971 - ★★★½
entry.content:
oliver reed steals a schoolteacher (candice bergen) because he wants to learn to read or something, only to have her wealthy husband (a slimy gene hackman) hunt down and pick off reed's crew a handful at a time, in this western that's equal parts peckinpah rip-off and bodice ripper.

the kidnapping, it turns out, rescues bergen from nights of marital rape at the hands of hackman, whose idea of vacation fun is branding a sex worker with his cigar. this genteel brutality is intercut with reed's gang slaughtering cattle to eat. the film trusts us to know who is the real monster, and to tell the difference between the several assaults reed rescues bergen from and the push-pull of her seduction at his hands.

it's a neat trick, actually, using the plot beats of the era's romance novels to thwart (and then, finally, horribly, confirm) the cynical nastiness of this era's westerns.

entry.title: The Debussy Film, 1965 - ★★★½
entry.content:
something like a teleological midpoint between the system (where ken russell discovered oliver reed) and another russell biopic for the bbc, dante’s inferno. reed plays an actor who is playing debussy in a film, which is a handy device for having the film-within-the-film’s director explain the composer’s life and complicated relationships. as the film and its film intertwine we get the sense that the french impressionists and the british beatniks weren’t really so different, or at least that russell wants us to think so. and fair enough, since it meant that russell could transition reed from the beats and hammer era of his career into his next, and best, phase. russell gave reed his art, as the latter once said, and it was to be an art of magnificent, troubled men.

entry.title: Castaway, 1986 - ★★★
entry.content:
an interesting though not always successful exploration of hetero gender politics when they are supposedly stripped of all the societal stuff that we think makes them untenable. it turns out that adam and eve in the garden of eden is actually a pretty toxic fantasy to try to bring to life.

for a movie with oliver reed as a horny middle aged weirdo and amanda donohoe as a young beauty who spends more than 2/3rds of the runtime naked, there's really nothing sexy about this film. the story is frustrating and deeply sad, and both reed and donohoe turn in astonishingly good work on what had to be a hellish shoot. (this was donohoe's second film ever!!)

entry.title: The System, 1964 - ★★★★
entry.content:
something like a proto-dirty dancing, this aching and bittersweet tale of sex, class, and rock 'n roll in a beachside tourist town stars oliver reed as an aloof working-class fuckboy—a "seaside don juan" as he puts it—who finally catches feelings and finds out that it sucks, actually.

he's quite good in the role, finally allowed to be a person instead of a werewolf or sociopath or a psychopath or a 17th-century scoundrel. he's also so beautiful i want to scratch my own eyes out. director michael winner and cinematographer nicolas roeg seem almost uninterested in the cast of gorgeous women littering the shots, so intent are they on capturing reed's eyes and mouth and chest (and ass, in one extra wide shot). winner cast reed 5 more times; 20 years after this, roeg tapped reed for his somewhat naughty island adventure, castaway.

wikipedia tells me that ken russell saw the system and cast reed in the debussy film—and in between the two films reed was jumped in a pub and had to get 63 stitches, resulting in the facial scars that he thought would end his career. ken russell knew better, of course.
